questions.prompt: A stable linear system is driven by a sinusoid that has been on for a long time. The steady output is
options: a sinusoid at the same frequency, scaled and shifted by \(G(j\omega)\)
a sinusoid at twice the input frequency
a constant equal to the DC gain, for any input frequency
a growing oscillation, because every sinusoid is an unstable mode
questions.explanation: For an asymptotically stable linear system the transients die, and the particular solution is a sinusoid at the driving frequency. Its scale is \(|G(j\omega)|\) and its phase shift is the angle of \(G(j\omega)\). Doubling the frequency would be a nonlinear effect. The DC gain applies only at \(\omega = 0\). A persistent sinusoid is an input, not a natural mode.

questions.explanation: \(G(j4) = 12/(3+j4)\), so \(|G| = 12/\sqrt{3^2+4^2} = 12/5 = 2.4\). The DC gain \(12/3 = 4\) drops the \(j4\) term. The reciprocal \(5/12\) inverts the magnitude.

questions.prompt: For the same \(G(s) = 12/(s+3)\) at \(\omega = 4\) rad/s, the phase of \(G(j\omega)\), in degrees, is
questions.explanation: The denominator \(3+j4\) has angle \(\tan^{-1}(4/3)\), and the numerator is positive, so the phase is \(-53.13^\circ\), stored as -53.1301. Reporting the positive angle drops the sign of a lag. Using the magnitude 2.4 as if it were a phase mixes the two parts of the complex value.

questions.prompt: Now \(G(s) = 5/(s+2)\) and the input is \(3\sin(2t)\). The steady-state output amplitude is
questions.explanation: \(|G(j2)| = 5/|2+j2| = 5/\sqrt{8}\). Times the input amplitude 3, the output amplitude is 5.3033. Reporting \(|G|\) alone forgets the input amplitude. Using the DC gain \(5/2 = 2.5\) times 3 gives 7.5 and ignores the \(j2\) term.

questions.figure_alt: A magnitude curve that falls as frequency rises.

questions.prompt: The frequency-response formula \(y(t) = |G(j\omega)|\,A\sin(\omega t + \angle G)\) requires the system to be
options: unstable, so that a natural mode can grow
asymptotically stable, so that every natural mode has died away
marginally stable, with a pole on the imaginary axis at \(j\omega\)
nonlinear, so that the amplitude can depend on \(A\)
questions.explanation: The formula is the forced response after the homogeneous solution has vanished. That happens when every eigenvalue has a negative real part. An unstable mode grows and swamps the sinusoid. A pole at \(j\omega\) resonates with the input and the amplitude is not given by a finite \(G(j\omega)\). Amplitude dependence on \(A\) is a nonlinear effect.
questions.figure_alt: A transient that dies toward a steady oscillation envelope.

questions.explanation: At \(\omega = 0\), \(G(0) = 8/2 = 4\). That is the DC gain. The high-frequency magnitude tends to 0, which is not the value at \(\omega = 0\). Twice the DC gain, 8, forgets the pole.

questions.figure_alt: One pole mark on the negative real axis.

questions.prompt: For a state-space model the same frequency response is
questions.explanation: Substituting \(s = j\omega\) into \(C(sI-A)^{-1}B+D\) gives the frequency response. Adding the four matrices is not that formula. The eigenvalues are the natural modes, not the response at one frequency. The matrix exponential is the free-response operator in time, not \(G(j\omega)\).

questions.explanation: The denominator at \(s = j3\) is \(10 - 9 + j6 = 1 + j6\), with magnitude \(\sqrt{37}\). Then \(|G| = 20/\sqrt{37} = 3.28798\). The DC gain \(20/10 = 2\) evaluates \(s = 0\). Using \(\omega_n = \sqrt{10}\) as the magnitude confuses the natural frequency with \(|G|\).

questions.figure_alt: A magnitude curve that falls as frequency rises.

questions.prompt: \(G(s) = (s+1)/(s+4)\). At \(\omega = 2\) rad/s the phase, in degrees, is
questions.explanation: The angle is \(\angle(1+j2) - \angle(4+j2)\). That difference is 36.8699 degrees. Each term is a lead, and the zero is closer to the origin, so the phase is positive. Adding the two angles instead of subtracting them is the angle of the product, not the quotient. The magnitude \(|G|\) is not a phase.

questions.prompt: A first-order lag has time constant \(0.25\) s. Its bandwidth, the frequency where the magnitude is \(1/\sqrt{2}\) of the DC gain, is
questions.explanation: For \(1/(\tau s+1)\) the bandwidth is \(1/\tau = 1/0.25 = 4\) rad/s. The time constant itself, 0.25, is not a frequency. Twice that corner, 8, is a different definition and not the \(-3\) dB point of a first-order lag.

questions.figure_alt: A flat magnitude that then falls.

questions.prompt: A pair of complex poles with a small damping ratio shows up in \(|G(j\omega)|\) as
options: a notch that goes to zero at the natural frequency
a magnitude that is exactly the DC gain at every frequency
a slope of \(-20\) dB/decade that never changes
a peak near the natural frequency
questions.explanation: Light damping produces a resonance peak near \(\omega_n\). A notch is a zero on the imaginary axis, not a lightly damped pole pair. The magnitude is not flat unless the damping is heavy and the zeros compensate the poles. A single real pole gives a slope near \(-20\) dB/decade; a complex pair eventually falls at \(-40\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 186" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>resonance peak</title><line x1="54" y1="140" x2="300" y2="140"/><polygon points="300,140 293.6,142.7 293.6,137.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="54" y1="140" x2="54" y2="28"/><polygon points="54,28 56.7,34.4 51.3,34.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="58" y="24" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">dB</text><polyline points="71,71.7 98.6,63.5 117.1,38.8 153.9,79.9 283,129.2" stroke-width="2.2"/><text x="300" y="156" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">f</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A magnitude curve with a hump before it falls.

questions.prompt: A scalar state-space model has \(A = -3\), \(B = 2\), \(C = 4\), \(D = 1\). At \(\omega = 2\) rad/s the magnitude of \(C(j\omega - A)^{-1}B + D\) is
questions.explanation: \(j\omega - A = 3 + j2\). Then \(C B /(j\omega-A) + D = 8/(3+j2) + 1\), whose magnitude is 3.10087. Dropping \(D\) leaves only the strict-feedthrough piece. Evaluating at \(\omega = 0\) gives \(8/3 + 1\), the DC gain, not the value at 2 rad/s.
